1004651.etyen:
Borrowed from German Hebraismus (“Hebraism”), based on Latin hebraeus (“Hebrew”) and -ismus (“-ism”). The Latin adjective is from Ancient Greek Ἑβραῖος (Hebraîos, “Hebrew”), probably via Aramaic עִבְרַי (ʿiḇray, “Hebrew”), from Biblical Hebrew עִבְרִי (ʿiḇrī, “Hebrew, Israelite”). The German suffix is from Latin -ismus (“-ism”), ultimately from Ancient Greek -ισμός (-ismós, “action- or process-forming suffix”).
Compare Danish hebraisme, Swedish hebraism and English Hebraism.

1004907.etyen:
From ministerråd (“council of ministers”) + møte (“meeting”), literally “council-of-ministers meeting”.
The first element, ministerråd (“council of ministers”), is itself formed from minister (“minister”) + råd (“council”). minister is borrowed from Latin minister (“servant, helper”), derived from minus (“less”). råd in the sense “council, assembly” continues Old Norse ráð, with influence in this sense from Middle Low German rāt (“council”) and Latin consilium (“council, deliberation”).
The second element, møte (“meeting”), is of Old Norse origin, related to mót (“meeting, encounter”) and mǿta
